passages.t: Miriam dies, and Moses strikes the rock
passages.happening:
“In the first month, the whole congregation of Israel entered the Wilderness of Zin and stayed in Kadesh. There Miriam died and was buried” (verse 1).

There is no water. The people gather against Moses and Aaron and say, ‘Why have you led us up out of Egypt to bring us to this wretched place?’ (verse 5). Moses and Aaron go to the entrance of the tent and fall facedown, and the glory of the LORD appears (verse 6).

God tells Moses, “Take the staff and assemble the congregation. You and your brother Aaron are to speak to the rock while they watch, and it will pour out its water” (verse 8).

Moses takes the staff and gathers the people. He says, “Listen now, you rebels, must we bring you water out of this rock?” (verse 10). “Then Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff, so that a great amount of water gushed out” (verse 11).

“But the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, ‘Because you did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites, you will not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them’” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Between chapters 19 and 20 almost forty years pass in silence. The first verse names a month and no year. But a later chapter dates Aaron's death, at the end of this chapter, to the fortieth year after the exodus (33:38), so most interpreters take this to be the fortieth year. Some think an earlier stay at Kadesh is meant. The children who were small at the time of the scouts are now grown.

The chapter begins and ends with a death. Miriam had watched over her baby brother at the Nile and had led Israel's song at the sea (Exodus 15:20-21). Her death is told in one short sentence. The generation that left Egypt is passing, and its leaders are passing with it.

Then the old complaint returns in almost the old words. The children sound like their parents. A reader might expect the old result: anger, judgment, a prayer. This time something different happens. God shows no anger at the people at all. He simply tells Moses how to give them water.

The story deliberately recalls an earlier one. Near the start of the wilderness years, at a place also called Meribah, God told Moses to strike a rock, and water came out (Exodus 17:1-7). Here the command is different. Moses is to take the staff, but he is to speak to the rock.

What Moses does is told in a few words. He calls the people rebels. He says ‘must we bring you water’. And he strikes the rock twice. Water pours out all the same. The people and their animals drink. God does not punish the thirsty for their leader's fault.

Then comes the sentence on Moses and Aaron. The hard question below asks what the fault was.

The place names carry the lesson. Meribah means quarreling. Kadesh comes from the Hebrew root for ‘holy’. Verse 13 says that there God ‘showed His holiness among them’. And the verb for rebelling cuts both ways. Moses calls the people rebels in verse 10. In verse 24 God uses the same verb for what Moses and Aaron did.
passages.later:
The Psalms remember the day with sympathy for Moses: “At the waters of Meribah they angered the LORD, and trouble came to Moses because of them. For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips” (Psalm 106:32-33).

Moses asked God to change the sentence, and was refused: “That is enough,” the LORD said. “Do not speak to Me again about this matter” (Deuteronomy 3:26). He was allowed to see the land from a mountain.

Paul says of Israel in the wilderness that ‘they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ’ (1 Corinthians 10:4). He means that the one who gave Israel water in the desert is the one the church knows as Christ.
passages.hard:
What exactly did Moses do wrong, and why was the punishment so heavy?

The text does not spell it out, and readers have given several answers, often together.

Some look at the act. God said to speak to the rock, and Moses struck it, twice. He went back to the way of Exodus 17 when he had been given a new command.

Some look at the words. Moses said ‘must we bring you water’, as if he and Aaron were the source. The psalm remembers that he ‘spoke rashly with his lips’.

Some look at the anger. God had shown no anger at the people that day. By calling them rebels, Moses made God appear angry when God meant only to give.

God's own verdict names the root. Moses and Aaron ‘did not trust Me to show My holiness in the sight of the Israelites’. In front of the whole people, the two men who spoke for God gave a false picture of him.

Why so heavy a consequence for one failure after forty years of faithfulness? Many readers answer that leaders are judged more strictly, because what they do shapes how a whole people sees God. The New Testament says the same of teachers (James 3:1).

It should also be seen what the sentence was not. Moses was not cast off. He went on leading Israel. God went on speaking with him. He saw the land from Mount Nebo before he died (Deuteronomy 34). And the Gospels show him standing in that land at last, talking with Jesus on the mountain (Matthew 17:3). The loss was real, and the chapter does not soften it. But Moses ended his life as God's friend.

Some Christian readers add that the rock, struck once in Exodus 17, did not need to be struck again, and see in that an echo of Christ's death once for all (Hebrews 9:28). The text does not say this. It is a later reflection.
passages.asks: Moses had carried this people for forty years, and he broke at the same old complaint. Ask what long-borne weight is making you sharp with the people you serve. And ask whether, in your anger, you have ever made God seem harsher to others than he is.

passages.happening:
From Kadesh, Moses sends messengers to the king of Edom. “This is what your brother Israel says: You know all the hardship that has befallen us” (verse 14). He tells of Egypt, of the cry to the LORD, and of the rescue.

Then he asks: “Please let us pass through your land” (verse 17). Israel will keep to the King's Highway, will not cross a field or vineyard, and will not drink from a well.

“But Edom answered, ‘You may not travel through our land, or we will come out and confront you with the sword’” (verse 18). Israel offers to pay for any water. Edom refuses again and comes out with a large army. “So Edom refused to allow Israel to pass through their territory, and Israel turned away from them” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea. Its people were descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob (Genesis 36). That is why Moses' message begins ‘your brother Israel’. The two nations were family.

The King's Highway was the main road running north and south through the highlands east of the Jordan. A request to pass along it was an ordinary piece of diplomacy, and Moses' message follows the usual form: who is writing, the story so far, the request, and the promises. In a dry land water belonged to whoever held the well, so Israel offers to pay for every drink.

Edom's answer is a threat, and then an army. Between brothers this was an insult, and later prophets did not forget it.

Notice what Israel does. It turns away. There is no battle. Deuteronomy gives the reason. God told Israel not to provoke the people of Esau, ‘for I will not give you any of their land’ (Deuteronomy 2:5). He had given that hill country to Esau. Israel's promise was for one land, and it gave no claim on its neighbors.

So the road to Canaan becomes longer. Israel must go around.

How organized Edom was at this time is debated. Much of the evidence for a developed kingdom comes from later centuries, though Egyptian texts from the late second millennium BC already mention the people of Edom.
passages.later:
God's word about Edom in Deuteronomy is plain: “I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession” (Deuteronomy 2:5). And the law later commanded, “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

The short book of Obadiah speaks to Edom about a later betrayal of its brother: “Because of the violence against your brother Jacob, you will be covered with shame” (Obadiah 1:10).
passages.asks: Israel was refused by its own brother, and it turned away without a fight. Ask where you have been shut out by family, and what you did with the insult. And ask what longer road you may be asked to walk because you will not force your way through.

passages.happening:
Israel leaves Kadesh and comes to Mount Hor, near the border of Edom. God tells Moses and Aaron, “Aaron will be gathered to his people; he will not enter the land that I have given the Israelites, because both of you rebelled against My command at the waters of Meribah” (verse 24).

Moses is to bring Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain. “Remove Aaron’s priestly garments and put them on his son Eleazar” (verse 26).

They climb the mountain in the sight of the whole congregation. Moses takes the garments from Aaron and puts them on Eleazar, and Aaron dies there on the mountaintop (verse 28). “When the whole congregation saw that Aaron had died, the entire house of Israel mourned for him thirty days” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The chapter that began with Miriam's death ends with Aaron's. Of the three who led Israel out of Egypt, only Moses is left, and he knows that he will not cross over.

Aaron's death is told quietly. Three men climb a mountain: two old brothers and a son. The people watch from below. There is no struggle and no speech.

The garments are the center of the scene. The high priest's robes were described at length in Exodus 28, and wearing them was what marked the office. Moses had dressed Aaron in them on the day he was ordained. Now he takes them off his brother and puts them on his brother's son. Aaron sees it done before he dies. The priesthood does not die with its first holder.

‘Gathered to his people’ is the phrase Genesis uses for the deaths of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Aaron dies under the same sentence as Moses, outside the land. He also dies as a man who belongs with his fathers.

Israel mourns him for thirty days. It is the same honor later given to Moses (Deuteronomy 34:8). The people who had so often spoken against Aaron weep for him.

Where Mount Hor was is debated. An old tradition places it near Petra in modern Jordan. Many scholars look for it nearer Kadesh, since the text sets it on the border of Edom.
passages.later: Hebrews sees in the death of priests the limit of the old priesthood: “Now there have been many other priests, since death prevented them from continuing in office. But because Jesus lives forever, He has a permanent priesthood” (Hebrews 7:23-24). Aaron's robes had to pass to another. Hebrews says that the priesthood of Jesus never does.
passages.asks: Aaron watched his work pass to his son before he died. Ask what work of yours will have to be handed on, and whether you are getting someone ready to carry it. And ask whom you ought to honor now, while they live, whom you have mostly criticized.
